newsitem.title: UK: Mandela says Africa must not be exploited.
newsitem.headline: Mandela says Africa must not be exploited.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela appealed to western nations on Friday not to exploit Africa in a replay of colonialism as it prepares to take its place in the global economy.
Mandela made his appeal in his only public speech on the last day of a private visit during which he was given the freedom of Oxford and feted by the city's world famous university.
He told the Oxford Centre for Islamic Studies that economic growth and investment into Africa from outside should bring benefit to the continent's people and lasting development.

"It would be a cruel irony of history if Africa's actions to regenerate the continent were to unleash a new scramble for Africa which, like that of the 19th century, plundered the continent's wealth and left it once more the poorer," Mandela said.

But Mandela told around 1,000 academics, students and diplomats that by pooling sovereignty in regional economic blocs, as a forerunner of an African Economic Union, African states could make themselves heard.

Mandela, who turns 79 on July 18, also appealed for cooperation between Moslems, Christians and followers of African religions, saying solidarity between different faiths had helped end apartheid in South Africa.
The South African President, who met Prime Minister Tony Blair on Thursday, left the theatre for a private dinner also attended by Prince Charles.
Police had set up road blocks in the centre and appealed to crowds not to mob the president.

But Mandela, accompanied by his companion, Graca Machel, the widow of former Mozambican president Samora Machel, was cheered by thousands of people as he drove from event to event in the university city.
Mandela was first taken to Oxford Town Hall where he was given the freedom of the city.

He was then welcomed by the University of Oxford in a special ceremony in front of leading academics. Mandela was awarded an honorary doctorate of civil law by the university at a special ceremony at Buckingham Palace a year ago.
But apart from the speech, all of the events were behind closed doors, with press and public excluded.
The honours for Mandela followed a day in which Machel was the focus of attention.

Machel, an international ambassador for children's rights who has accompanied Mandela on most of his recent travels, was awarded an honorary degree by Essex University for her study of the effects of war on children.
The couple were taking advantage of the South African government's mid-winter recess.
They are due to travel on from Britain, where they arrived on Tuesday, to Indonesia and Thailand before returning to Africa.
